column2: How can we provide every car owner one place to book, access, and pay for services?
column3: The "EV Pass": one identity, one wallet, one place for everything travel-related for car owners. The sequence to solve is book ? access ? pay, with AI making the whole process feel effortless.
column4: The EV charging market is crowded but undifferentiated — most solutions do roughly the same thing, and that fragmentation is the real pain for drivers: too many apps and providers, and time and money lost just to charge. The proposed fix is an AI-powered platform that joins drivers and cities into a single charging experience — real-time map discovery, identity-based access, and a digital wallet. It matters most to EV owners and motorists, with parking operators, electricity providers, and fleets gaining alongside them. For the sprint, Rollyy is after an unfiltered outside read on the vision.
column5: A Finnish startup set on making life easier for EV and car owners. Its current platform gives access to mobile charging robots in parking lots: users book a session via app, the robot drives itself to the vehicle, and charging happens automatically. (www.rollyy.com)
column6: The complete playbook from start to finish — guidance, ideas, instructions, and Rollyy's vision for the ecosystem — plus access to Rollyy's API. Known integration paths are there to build on rather than rebuild (Google Pay, Apple Pay), so nothing heavy needs inventing. Incentives include five days at Epicenter and access to ecosystem events.
column7: Something that runs live in Rollyy's sandbox, not a deck. It should carry the one-flow experience end to end and treat AI as the engine — a voice or agentic assistant, MCP — rather than a feature glued on top. Crucially it adds no new app or provider to the pile and wastes none of the user's time or money, leaning on existing rails like Apple Pay or Google Pay. The cases that win pair an original angle on where Rollyy could go with a group that clearly worked well together.

column2: How can we make employees' learning journeys engaging, so they are guided and matched with the most relevant learning offerings?
column3: Design part of a learning aggregator that pulls people in instead of pushing courses at them. The nut to crack: give each user a motivating, adaptive professional journey — linking a company's sustainability goals to job roles at every level, then guiding them through steps that feed curiosity, build real skills, and turn learning into sustainability action. AI is what makes that guidance feel personal and scale to everyone.
column4: Far more sustainability learning exists than anyone ever finds. It's scattered across MOOCs, courses, webinars, and events, and ESG sits off in its own silo rather than in daily work, so employees seldom see how it touches their role. The fallout is familiar: unfocused study, flat engagement, and a skills gap that resurfaces later as compliance risk and lost money. The remedy is to pull the scattered offerings together, tie sustainability goals to individual roles, and package it as a journey compelling enough to stick with. Employees and the companies and HR teams behind them stand to gain most, while sustainability managers, training and education providers, and the wider environment benefit further out.
column5: Learnsy, a Helsinki-based Finnish B2B platform founded in 2024, is devoted to sustainability and ESG learning. It neither hosts nor produces courses; instead it scouts and curates offerings worldwide and connects a company's ESG, CSRD, and SDG goals to employees' roles, interests, and current knowledge — turning strategy into guided journeys. The aim is to close the sustainability skills gap, drive measurable impact, and support compliance.
column6: Access to the Learnsy platform (demo credentials or similar) and raw data, an anonymised interview dataset, and the ESCO skills categories as a ready-made skills taxonomy. Open learning catalogues (MIT OpenLearning, a partner for the challenge, or EIT Campus) and example corporate targets such as large consultancies give reference points. The idea is to build on these sources, not assemble a catalogue yourself.
column7: A functioning MVP a real company or learning institution could roll out — built, not pitched. AI should be doing real work here, reading behaviour in the platform to guide and motivate each person, not a chatbot bolted onto a course list. Engagement is the whole point: storytelling that fits the journey, a true "wow" moment, and progress data people can track and compare over time. You'd know it worked from returning users, finished courses, and genuine adoption. An inventive reading of Learnsy's vision, delivered by a team in sync, is where a case earns its edge.

column2: How can we find manual work that can be automated across an organisation, so companies can focus on automating high-value problems?
column3: An AI layer that surfaces the manual, repetitive work hiding across an organisation's departments and turns it into ranked candidates for automation. The path to nail is discover ? prioritise; actually building or running the automation is out of scope. Underneath it all is money — time and value bled away by repetitive tasks, human error, delays, and clunky processes.
column4: Most automation efforts stall at the very first step: no one knows where the automatable work actually sits. It's thinly spread across finance, HR, operations, and customer teams, and rarely gets raised because each task feels too minor to mention. The fix is an AI-driven way to locate and rank that work — ideally inferring the opportunities from organisational signals, data, or workflows instead of waiting for employees to spell them out. It serves people stuck in manual-heavy roles and the SMEs and enterprises employing them (freeing them for higher-value work, not replacing them), with operations and IT teams benefiting too.
column5: Cognovo, a Finnish company built around AI-powered integration and automation, connects enterprise and SME systems — ERP, CRM, HR, finance, and custom apps — into one ecosystem and automates the repetitive work that runs across them.
column6: Start from the partner's tip: hunt for the manual operations companies quietly run across departments — that's where the automatable work hides. Cognovo brings its own automation know-how and process templates so teams can build against realistic workflows, and it leaves teams free to chase whatever signals or data reveal how work truly happens inside an organisation.
column7: A runnable MVP showing an approach a real customer could adopt, beyond a presentation. It should trace discover ? prioritise from one end to the other, with AI earning its keep — spotting patterns, reasoning about how work flows, weighing value and feasibility — rather than playing chatbot. It shouldn't lean on heavy customer input; the more it uncovers on its own, the better. And it should bite into real pain: wasted hours, errors, delays, cost. A new perspective on Cognovo's direction, from a group that plainly clicked, lifts a case out of the pack.

column2: How can we show how actions affect the longevity of household items, so customers feel motivated about the lifecycle of the things they own?
column3: Care Loop's vision is conscious ownership: scan a product, grasp its real impact, and keep it in use for as long as possible. The stubborn part is the use phase — once the product is owned, how do you turn the data it throws off into something that keeps people engaged and motivated to extend its life, well beyond a single repair or resale, with AI taking the effort out of it?
column4: Shoppers drown in product information yet have little reason to trust it: at the till they meet more detail than they can weigh, default to price, and stay suspicious of claims that smell like greenwashing. The data is scattered, even as rules such as the EU Digital Product Passport begin demanding trustworthy, structured information. Care Loop answers with an AI platform that scans a product, scores its true impact on a Conscious Index (health, planet, ethics, longevity), then acts — repair, resell, recycle — inside one connected loop, with a Product Passport that follows the item. Buyers and owners gain the most, and retailers, brands, manufacturers, insurers and service providers, cities, communities, and the planet gain with them.
column5: Care Loop helps people buy less, own better, and waste nothing. Anyone can scan a product to see what they're really buying, and the platform links everyone in the ownership chain — repair, refurbishment, resale, recycling — around keeping products in circulation. Every product carries a Conscious Index and a Product Passport that logs its care history and fills a resale listing automatically, so the next owner starts with verified trust.
column6: Care Loop opens up its conscious-ownership toolkit: product segments, consumer personas, user journeys and features, a working demo, and the trust score and Conscious Index view. Teams also get background on the Digital Product Passport and EU regulation to design against — the goal being a data structure that could feed a real passport, not a throwaway prototype.
column7: A clearly defined way to structure and classify product data so it could later slot into a Digital Product Passport, with AI doing genuine work through scanning, scoring, or an agentic assistant rather than tacked on at the end. It should make the pull of everyday actions on a product's lifespan visible enough that owners actually want to look after what they own. An honest, independent take on Care Loop's vision from a team that gels is the real differentiator.

column2: How can we learn from proven leaders, so new innovators build on what works rather than reinvent everything?
column3: Proteins.1 has the science; from the sprint it wants the map. Trace how the winners in life science and diagnostics genuinely reached the market, then convert that into a clear read on market trends and clinical openings for a breakthrough technology. The tangle is data: there's plenty of it, the way to look at it is still forming, and the gap between deep tech and its customers has to be closed with evidence, not guesswork.
column4: Deep tech and its customers often sit at opposite ends of one problem: the science can run years ahead of anything on the market while the people who'd benefit have no easy way to find, trust, or buy it. The live questions are practical — when does a technology stop being a research result and become a product, what did the companies that broke through actually do, and how should a young team read its own data so the answers hold up? The sprint's output is a market and clinical opportunity map, using AI to make quick sense of the terrain: who the established players are, which applications carry the most value, the fastest routes to adoption, and what the paths of successful innovators reveal.
column5: A Finnish deep-tech diagnostics company spun out of VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland. It has built a physics-based, enzyme-free platform that amplifies and reads single protein molecules, detecting biomarkers across DNA, RNA, and proteins from very small samples at a sensitivity current instruments can't reach — often described as doing for proteins what PCR did for DNA, minus the enzymes. Early applications target oncology, neurology, and immunology in research, with regulated clinical diagnostics to follow.
column6: Proteins.1 walks teams through how it currently reads the market and its data, with worked examples of companies that scaled well, so no one starts from nothing. The people behind the technology — microfluidics, photonics, and regulated medical devices — are on hand to explain where the science stands and what a realistic route to product looks like.
column7: A map a team could put straight to work — a market and clinical opportunity map, not a sweeping industry essay. It should set out a clear, repeatable way to read the data, name the leaders worth studying and pin down exactly what made them succeed, and point to the applications and market routes where Proteins.1 gains most. AI should do the collecting, structuring, and interpreting rather than sit there as decoration, and the whole thing should stay tight enough to act on. A well-argued outside view and a team pulling together separate a strong case from the rest.
